article.headline: The Gap is the Product: Inside the 'Convention-Reality' Arbitrage Framework That Claims to Be Too Dangerous to Name
article.lede: A screenshot circulating on X shows a prototype tool called ArbitrageDiscover OPT 4.7 that promises to identify market segments where billing conventions have survived long past the economic realities that once justified them. The example it reaches for — $450-an-hour associates doing due diligence that AI can replicate in ninety seconds for under two dollars — is not hypothetical.
article.body:
Carlos E. Perez, who writes and posts under the handle @IntuitMachine, has spent more than a decade building a body of work around the idea that human cognition systematically misreads fast-moving technological change. His Medium publication, Intuition Machine, treats AI less as a product category than as a pressure system bearing down on institutional habits. ArbitrageDiscover OPT 4.7, the tool glimpsed in the screenshots he shared, appears to be an early-stage or experimental instrument — there is no indexed public repository, no product page, and no independent documentation — that operationalizes one of Perez's recurring arguments: that the most durable economic opportunities of the next few years will be found not in building new things but in locating places where the price of old things has not yet adjusted to new costs.

The interface shown in the screenshots is built around a concept the tool calls the "convention-reality gap" — the distance between what a system assumes about itself and what is actually true about it. The framing will be familiar to anyone who has spent time in strategic-mapping circles. Simon Wardley's influential methodology for charting value chains distinguishes between where a component sits on the evolution curve (from genesis through custom build to product to commodity) and where a firm's internal map wrongly places it. The ArbitrageDiscover tool appears to formalize a similar intuition: map any market's components onto a custom/commodity/reference axis, identify the components where convention still treats something as custom that the market has quietly reduced to a commodity, and the gap between the two is the arbitrage. The tool's own jargon — "K-traces," "CV Capture," "Cascade Corruption," "Single-Mode Blindness," "Collapse Cost Asymmetry" — suggests a more elaborated internal vocabulary, though without source documentation it is impossible to assess whether these terms carry precise definitions or serve mainly as atmospheric texture.

The legal services example embedded in the screenshots is the clearest illustration of the underlying thesis, and it happens to be well-supported by independent evidence. A 2025 survey by Axiom of more than 600 senior legal leaders found that 79 percent of law firms now actively use AI tools — yet only 6 percent charge clients less for AI-assisted work, and 34 percent charge more. Law firm revenue jumped 13 percent in 2024, with net income rising 17 percent. The efficiency gains from AI are, in other words, being captured almost entirely by firms rather than passed to clients. The tool's "dossier" for its legal example — $450-per-hour associate billing, a 2019 cost basis, monthly partner review — describes precisely this structure: a pricing convention that hardened when the underlying cost of first-pass document analysis was genuinely expensive and has not softened since the cost collapsed. Axiom's data confirm that 94 percent of in-house legal leaders want alternative fee models; only the firms have not yet been forced to offer them at scale. The gap is real.

Perez's framing of this as "too dangerous to release" warrants scrutiny. The phrase is classic hype inoculation — a rhetorical move that simultaneously signals seriousness and manufactures urgency — and it should be treated skeptically on its own terms. The methodology described in the screenshots is not a weapon; it is a structured checklist for a form of strategic analysis that management consultants, venture investors, and Wardley-map practitioners have been doing informally for years. What ArbitrageDiscover appears to add is a systematic vocabulary for the exercise and, if the interface is functional, a workflow that guides a user through the mapping steps without requiring fluency in the underlying theory. That is a genuine contribution to accessibility, but it is not dangerous in any meaningful sense. The danger framing likely reflects Perez's observation — correct, on the evidence — that the window for acting on these gaps is narrowing fast: once the convention has adjusted to the reality, the arbitrage closes.

The deeper and more interesting claim in the tool's tagline — "value lives in the gap between what a system assumes about itself and what is actually true about it" — is essentially a restatement of a problem that institutional economics has studied under various labels for decades. Joseph Schumpeter called the force that destroys the gap "creative destruction." Clayton Christensen mapped it as the trajectory of a disruptive entrant from the low end of a market. The ArbitrageDiscover framework is notably different in orientation: it is not primarily interested in how the disruption happens, but in who captures the economic surplus in the period between when an old cost structure becomes obsolete and when pricing finally reflects that fact. In legal due diligence, that period may be measured in years. In faster-moving markets — software licensing, content production, basic financial analysis — it may already be closing. The tool's value, to the extent it has value, is in training a user's eye to spot the lag before the consensus does.

concepts.definition: The ArbitrageDiscover framework's term for the distance between what a market or institution assumes about its own cost structure and what is actually true — the gap that persists when pricing conventions survive long after the underlying economics that justified them have been disrupted.

In its classical financial meaning, arbitrage is the simultaneous purchase and sale of an asset in two markets to profit from a price difference. ArbitrageDiscover uses the term more broadly: any durable mismatch between the price a market charges for a service and the true marginal cost of delivering it — a gap that a well-positioned entrant can exploit.

A strategic framework developed by Simon Wardley that plots components of a value chain against an evolution axis running from novel (genesis) through custom-built to commodity. It is used to identify where a firm's internal assumptions about which capabilities are strategic versus routine diverge from market reality — the same diagnostic intent as ArbitrageDiscover's custom/commodity/reference axis.

The additional cost of running one more AI query on a hosted language model — typically a fraction of a cent for a standard task. The tool's legal example contrasts this figure (cited as under $2 for a first-pass due-diligence summary) against the $450-per-hour associate rate to illustrate the scale of the convention-reality gap.

One of ArbitrageDiscover's internal vocabulary terms, apparently referring to the structural imbalance between how quickly AI can collapse the cost of a service and how slowly the market's pricing conventions adjust — the asymmetry that creates and sustains the arbitrage window.

article.fact_check: The 'too dangerous to release' framing in the original tweet is theatrical rather than substantive. The convention-reality gap methodology is a repackaging of well-established strategic analysis traditions — Wardley mapping, Christensonian disruption theory, and basic microeconomic cost-price lag — assembled into a structured interface. Nothing about the approach is novel enough to constitute a genuine risk. The legal due diligence example is, however, empirically grounded: Axiom's 2025 survey of 600-plus legal leaders confirms that 79 percent of law firms use AI while only 6 percent pass savings to clients, and Fennemore's billing analysis documents the structural pressure toward fixed-fee models. The tool's 90-second, sub-$2 AI diligence claim is directionally accurate given documented AI inference costs and the performance of current legal AI platforms. ArbitrageDiscover OPT 4.7 itself has no indexed public repository or independent documentation as of May 2026, making it impossible to evaluate whether the full feature set (K-traces, CV Capture, Cascade Corruption, Single-Mode Blindness) reflects a coherent formal system or an evocative vocabulary layered over a relatively simple mapping exercise.

poster_intuitmachine.bio: Writer and theorist focused on AI cognition, multi-agent architectures, and the structural consequences of machine learning for institutions. Publishes the Intuition Machine blog on Medium. Topics include Quaternion Process Theory, Artificial Intuition, and the epistemology of fast-moving technological change.
